comparison: Both strongly support the main N45 finding during pain (C3, C4, C58, C59, C62, C64). OpenEval emphasizes statistical convergence across multiple approaches with strong Bayesian evidence. Peer reviewers describe this as 'convincing evidence' and 'the main outcome.' Peer result also includes C63, which OpenEval evaluates separately as uncertain (R8).

Perfect agreement on sham TMS control experiment (C5, C75, C76, C77). Both evaluations support that the control effectively ruled out auditory and somatosensory confounds. OpenEval notes moderate Bayesian evidence; peer reviewers state this 'strengthens the conclusion.'

Perfect agreement on subthreshold TMS control experiment (C6, C79, C80, C81). Both support that this ruled out reafferent feedback as a mechanism. OpenEval cites moderate Bayesian evidence; peer reviewers affirm this 'strengthens the conclusion that the N45 TEP peak could be implicated in the perception of painful stimuli.'

Both support the GABAergic interpretation and biomarker potential (C7, C86-C89). OpenEval notes the mechanistic link relies on prior literature rather than direct pharmacological manipulation. Peer result also includes synthesis claims (C8, C9, C99, C112-C114) that OpenEval evaluates separately (R5), and reviewers describe interpretation as 'adequate' and 'convincing.'

Overlapping support for main findings synthesis (C8, C9, C99, C112-C114). OpenEval emphasizes replication across experiments and individual-level correlations while noting predictive utility requires validation. Peer reviewers accept the biomarker interpretation and find the overall conclusions convincing.

Perfect agreement on MEP-pain correlation findings (C51, C52, C102, C103). Both support the robust correlation with strong Bayesian evidence. OpenEval notes weak group-level effect with high individual variability; peer reviewers confirm consistency with prior systematic reviews without objection.

Perfect agreement on temporal control analyses (C60, C61, C111). Both support that lack of pre-pain vs. post-pain differences strengthens pain-specific interpretation. OpenEval explicitly evaluates this; peer reviewers implicitly accept by endorsing specificity of pain effects without raising temporal confound concerns.

Perfect agreement on N45 reliability data (C82-C85). Both support good to excellent ICC values. OpenEval explicitly notes this strengthens biomarker potential; peer reviewers implicitly endorse by stating 'results are convincing' and 'paradigm and analysis are sound.'

Divergent evaluations of pain rating variability (C43-C46, C108). OpenEval supports this as an acknowledged limitation with clear statistical evidence. Peer reviewers show uncertainty, with one suggesting additional controls for stimulus intensity/salience, implying concern about whether N45 changes are pain-specific versus reflecting general stimulus properties.

Both support TMS-EEG methodological advantages (C23-C25, C29). OpenEval evaluates background claims about technique advantages with citations. Peer reviewers affirm 'main strength' is combined TMS-EEG approach and note it 'opens the way for exploration of cortical excitability outside M1 in acute pain.'

Both express uncertainty about secondary TEP findings (C65-C67). OpenEval notes moderate evidence in Experiment 1, lack of replication, and no correlation with pain ratings. Peer result also includes dissociation findings (C68-C70) that OpenEval evaluates separately (R11). Peer reviewers implicitly accept these null/weak findings by focusing on positive N45 results.

Overlapping evaluation of MEP-TEP dissociation (C68-C70). OpenEval supports dissociable responses with Bayesian evidence, noting importance for understanding different pain processing aspects. Peer reviewers did not challenge these findings, implicitly accepting the pattern showing N45 specificity.

OpenEval expresses uncertainty about source localization results (C53-C57) due to acknowledged methodological limitations (no co-registered MRI, no electrode digitization, no between-condition comparisons). No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports differential MEP/N45 correlations with pain ratings (C107), noting opposite correlation directions highlight complexity of pain-related cortical processes. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports basic sensory testing validation (C36-C42) as essential methodological validation confirming appropriate stimulus parameters. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports synthesis of prior GABAergic mechanisms literature (C90-C97), noting this represents background knowledge rather than new findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
